title: RM Sotheby's
note:
Captured as the working example for the auction-catalog register that skills/typography-taste borrows from. The hero is the right idea: full-bleed night photography, and the lot text sits in a translucent grey scrim block in the lower left rather than being centred over the image — the scrim is doing the legibility work, exactly the escalation ladder in skills/color-taste §5.

The title is set in a high-contrast serif with true typographic quotes ('The Pop Art F1'), the supporting lines drop to a neutral grotesque, and the date/venue line goes smallest — three registers in a four-line block, which is the whole editorial-contrast idea in miniature.

Where it falls short of a rating 3: the nav is a plain uppercase grotesque row with no tracking discipline, VIEW LOT is an underlined text link inside a scrim (a banned pattern — it reads as prose, not as an action), and the carousel arrows are large chrome overlays on the photograph. The lot plate below the fold is closer to a generic e-commerce grid than to a printed catalog page. Useful for the hero treatment; not a model for the rest.

Anti-reference — exceptional automotive assets trapped inside a generic corporate-luxury CMS. The hero relies almost entirely on photography, while the rest of the page collapses into repetitive card grids, mechanical 50/50 bands, cosmetic luxury typography, weak micro-hierarchy, and arbitrary tonal alternation. There is no sustained dominant-subordinate-support relationship after the hero. Negative space acts as passive separation rather than an active compositional shape. Image directions fail to build a continuous eye path, tonal masses fragment between modules, and the repeated card cadence becomes metronomic. The grid measures correctly without composing meaningfully. Premium content alone does not create premium art direction.

title: The Gentlewoman
note:
The reference case for air as status: the landing page is one viewport tall and roughly three-quarters empty — a single magazine cover centred in white, nav above, one caption line below. Nothing competes, so the cover reads as an object rather than as content.

Worth stealing: (1) the footer caption is the only sentence on the page and it carries the entire editorial message, sitting on a hairline rule with the pagination at the far right — metadata as composition; (2) the photography is black-and-white, which is what lets a single saturated accent work without the page becoming about colour.

CONTRADICTION worth keeping: this breaks skills/color-taste on two counts — the accent is a bright saturated turquoise, well above the chroma ceiling, and it IS the identity rather than a setting (nav, logo, rules, caption, all of it). It works because the accent is the *only* colour in an otherwise monochrome world, so the restraint has moved from the hue to the palette size. Evidence that the rule's real mechanism is "one colour, ruthlessly" rather than "low chroma" — flag for the next distillation run.

Also note the display face is a rounded geometric grotesque, not a serif. Editorial authority here comes from scale and space, not from a didone.

OUT — The cover image has the right to exist as a standalone editorial composition. As a website, the project fails. The desktop navigation is ugly, the footer is unresolved, and the initial visual idea never develops into a coherent web experience. One decent cover does not make this a design reference.
